1	# 39 unconventional ideas that will rewire your brain
2	
3	Each of these should alter the way you see things - upgrade your mental software. From climate change to aging and common patterns among business, biology, and physics.
4	
5	I collect ideas from books, thoughts, anecdotes, and through observation. 
6	This will be a long read. At the end, the full list will be included. Feel free to skip to the tl;dr and share, or bookmark for the full read later.
7	
8	## **1.** **If you find a genius, give them all power**
9	
10	There come times in life when you encounter extraordinary individuals - people whose abilities are well in excess of your own. A handful of those times, you’ll also recognize a deeply moral drive. It doesn’t happen very often. It might only happen 1-5 times in a lifetime. But you need to be on the lookout. When you come across one of these people, partner with them.
11	
12	Studying the life of Lee Kuan Yew flabbergasted me. Singapore was a malarial swamp. No common culture, no people, and no country wanted to help them at the beginning. Citizens didn’t even speak the same language. Then this man came along and he single-handedly fixed all societal issues, turning Singapore into one of the richest countries in the world by per capita GDP. LKY couldn’t have done it alone; he had a great team of ministers and advisors. That’s another feature of these astounding individuals: they know how to build an exceptional team.
13	
14	Warren Buffett became Berkshire’s CEO in the late '60s. He turned a mediocre $15M textile operation into a $1 trillion conglomerate, while earning essentially no salary and partnering with Charlie Munger. 
15	Imagine you knew a young Buffett. The single decision of handing him your money would make you end up billions of dollars richer. And you wouldn't have to lift a finger.
16	
17	A Buffett or Lee Kuan Yew kind of talent might come once every century. And in all likelihood, we won’t meet people like them. But the idea holds true at all levels. Think of that marketing agency whose performance is 2-3x that of the other agency you hire. Think of the person who manages 1-2 people, but whose results are astounding and could manage 10-50. Think of your incredibly smart friend who could and would do a lot but has no resources. Life becomes easier as you stack tailwinds.
18	
19	## **2. You are neither right nor wrong because a poll agrees with you**
20	
21	You are right because your facts and reasoning are right; because the outcome was similar to what you predicted. Other people’s opinions has nothing to do with the truth. Truth lives by itself. It’s independent.
22	
23	Until Darwin, all naturalists believed in the independent creation of species. After Darwin, almost no one did. Everyone thought the world had been created 5,000 years ago; after Lyell published his work, no one thinks that. Before Copernicus, people thought the Earth was at the center of the solar system. Before Galileo, that a heavy stone fell faster than a light one.
24	
25	What society holds true at any point in time is fragile. It only takes one observation to shatter it completely and for a new paradigm to emerge.
26	
27	When Henry Singleton took over Teledyne, dividends were the only conceivable way in which companies could return capital to their shareholders. He figured that, done well, buybacks could create more value and proceeded to repurchase shares when multiples contracted in the 70s. Thereafter, everyone on Wall Street caught up with their tax efficiency and started doing share buybacks periodically. In the 90s, Singleton had his last interview and was asked what he thinks of this development:
28	
29	> “If everyone is doing them, then there must be something wrong with them.”
30	## **3. The key to success is mediocre competition**
31	
32	You are always competing with someone. For attention, a position, a candidate, a customer, an audience. Every activity, meal, or plan competes with every other, time being the only true asset.
33	
34	Winning can be a win-win, but that doesn’t mean there isn't a loser somewhere. Imagine you pitch your product or service to a potential customer. After your meeting, the customer meets another vendor. What determines whether you win is not only your performance, the quality of your service, and soft skills, but also how they compare to your competitor’s. How much easier it’d be if their product weren't functional or they didn't show up?
35	
36	It’s not about taking advantage of other people. It’s about being smart at game selection. You’ll end up competing anyway, so you might as well pick something where you have an edge over other people. You must be capable of telling where your edge comes from. At a poker table, ‘if you don’t know who the patsy is 30 minutes into the game, then you are the patsy’.
37	
38	Niches are large enough to support a family and fund growth. If there is demand, and you control a tier of the supply, you’ll do well. Doesn’t matter if you’re Alaska’s best fisherman. If you’re the best at something for which there’s stable demand, you’ll do well. Buffett oftentimes said that the best shield against inflation is being the best lawyer or doctor in town; your earnings are protected because you supply the market with a high quality product that’s continuously in demand.
39	
40	## **4. There are answers worth billions of dollars in a $30 history book** **- Munger**
41	
42	Near the end of his life, Charlie Munger often told an anecdote later in life: 
43	he read an investment magazine every year for 30-40 years and had never found an actionable idea in it... until the 2010s. Charlie subsequently invested a couple million in the business portrayed and took out $80M in profit. He gave that $80M to Li Lu and Li Lu turned it into ~$400M. All of this in the span of under 15 years, I believe.
44	
45	That’s how powerful reading can be, especially in investing. It only takes one idea to change your life. Imagine if you knew everything you now know when you were 10-20 years old. Would you exercise? Would you invest? Would you read? Would you spend more time with relatives?
46	
47	You are not smarter than your former self. You’re just more knowledgeable, hopefully wiser. Knowledge is power; it brings profit in all shapes and forms. And the best thing is that it is, to a large extent, ‘speed-runnable.’ Read 1,000 carefully selected books and I suspect decisions become simpler. It’s immaterial if you read those 1,000 books in one decade or six decades. I strongly suspect you’ll take away most insights anyway. The difference is that you have that mental database to compound and work for you for five decades thereafter.
48	
49	You don’t need to make all mistakes there are to be made. Learn from people who came before you; avoid the mistakes they made and take their advice. Life is very much the same in many ways. And you don’t have to figure out Newton’s laws by yourself; you won’t be able to, or you’ll spend your whole life trying. Just read about them. It’s a fair shortcut.
50	
51	## **5. It’s always a skill issue**
52	
53	If you don’t get what you want in the long run, it’s likely on you. This is especially true nowadays, when opportunities are widespread; the internet and now AI have leveled the playing field.
54	
55	This reframe is extremely impactful and pragmatic.   From: It’s another person’s fault.  To: It’s my fault. If it didn’t turn out the way I wanted, I could’ve done something better.
56	
57	It’s a reframe about responsibility and accountability. If you take it, you'll learn something from it. And your behavior will thereafter be more profitable. You can always do something better. You can always be better. Failed at an interview? Maybe my English or knowledge are off. Failed at an exam? I didn't study hard enough. Don't know how to close a customer? I'm not a good enough salesperson yet.
58	
59	There's always someone who could do what we're supposed to do better than us. And not because they were born with it. They acquired the skill.
60	
61	> "The easiest way to get what you want is to deserve what you want"
62	No one is a natural at anything. The rate of learning plays a big role in how quickly you arrive at a proficiency level and acquire new techniques. But not even the most remarkable human beings could've gone far without intense practice and focus.
63	
64	When I read da Vinci’s biography, I was astounded by his obsessive personality and the attention he gave to getting every little detail right.  Talent can only take you so far. There is no substitute for hard work.
65	
66	Whatever another person has, you can have (naturally limited to changeable things, which I’d estimate to be in excess of 97% of cravings). Some achievements and results take more effort and time, but there’s no rule why you can’t reach a certain summit.
67	
68	‘Aim for the sky. For, even if you don’t get there, you could reach the clouds.’ Improvement is deeply satisfactory, irrespective of whether you reach your original target. And time will pass anyway, so you might as well do something.
69	
70	## **6. Cargo Cult Science**
71	
72	Feynman gave this speech in the '70s. He warned the audience about the upcoming new ‘science’. They’ll say their conclusions have a scientific basis, that they followed the scientific method, and that their opinions are just as valid as those forged through sweat and tears in the fields of mathematics and physics.
73	
74	But they are non-knowers. They lack intellectual integrity and rigor, and ignore how difficult it is to produce any piece of knowledge. When trying to explain a phenomenon, the way to establish causality is by isolating variables in an experimental/observational manner and running tests.
75	
76	Some of these people don’t realize their disciplines fall into the complex adaptive systems realm. Many variables impact any given outcome, and all of them are interconnected. Isolation is virtually impossible. And true causality can’t be determined because the environment continuously changes; new set of rules, the experiment is no longer the same.
77	
78	Furthermore, if they do know this and insist on their newfound truth, it’s likely that they are not disclosing the whole picture. Failed experiments are left out of their papers and noisy data goes unreported. Only elements that validate the conclusion are presented.
79	
80	Beware of people who claim they know something that’s really hard to know. The best shield is to deeply research a topic. See for yourself how hard it is to stay on the tracks of truth to not misinform others. Or you can lie to yourself, and others will play along.
81	
82	> “The first principle is that you must not fool yourself - and you are the easiest person to fool."
83	## 7. **The men who can manage men manage the men who can manage only things, and the men who can manage money manage all - Durant**
84	
85	The output from your employed capacity is a function of how much leverage you have and how well you use each unit of time. If it’s only you getting paid per hour, earnings scale linearly with your input. If you have the eye or skill of a master, you might get paid per project or earn a share of the generated proceeds; output becomes nonlinear. If you manage people and get to decide how they employ their time at work, the foregoing multiplies. If you can manage money and understand returns on time, everything will be at your disposition.

87	## **8. Incentives**
88	
89	We repeat behavior that rewards us and avoid that which punishes us. No one wakes up wanting to bang their head into the wall. Pain is terror, in all forms. If a conversation with your friend was unpleasant, you won’t want to go through it again. And thus you might see that friend less often, even if the unpleasantness wasn’t out of a personal issue. We are wired this way.
90	
91	Man’s genome took billions of years to evolve. On an Earth were catastrophe abounds, mechanisms were built into our DNA to preserve ourselves. Everything in your circuitry is optimized for self-preservation and reproduction. What is pain if not the body telling you you’re being constrained in one way or another from the thing for which you live?
92	
93	If you want something to happen, align everyone’s interests toward it and it will. We only do things that are in our interest; the self-serving bias is too powerful. Generosity does exist but there’s truth to the idea that there’s no action that’s purely altruistic.
94	
95	> “Reason, justice and equity never had weight enough on the face of the earth, to govern the councils of men” – John Adams.
96	It is interest alone which does it.   When there are enough incentives, anything can happen. In the 1930s-40s in Russia, there were quotas to fill for arrests. It didn’t matter if people had done a wrongdoing. Quotas needed to be filled and any pretext was good enough.
97	
98	There was an organization with two products. One was higher quality and it didn’t sell for a much higher price, yet nobody bought it. After some inquiring, management realized salesmen received a higher commission if they sold the lower-quality product. Managers inverted the commission and sales of the higher-quality product eclipsed the other.

100	Pavlov ran thousands of experiments with dogs to investigate reflexes. Most tests had the secretion of saliva as the objective, which in a natural setting happens when food or poison enters the dog’s mouth. Pavlov found dozens of stimuli that could be conditioned to trigger this reflex. You can use the sound of a bell to trigger saliva. Organisms’ cabling can be reconfigured to suit your needs. Whose bread I eat, his song I sing.

Don’t ask your barber if you need a haircut.

104	I’ll finish this section with a story my father told me once.  He was working at a consulting firm and had a group meeting. The manager who was leading it arrived 5 minutes late. Then he pounds the table and says, 'Gentlemen, are we gonna do what’s right or what’s in our interest?'

106	## **9. Intelligent is different from smart, and both can be stupid**
107	
108	I think being smart is being quick of mind; smart people are witty; they compute/permutate quickly and are good at pattern-recognition at the micro level. Intelligence is broader, but holds less specific power. Intelligent people can see the depth to things; they know what questions are worth entertaining and can hold one in their heads for days until they get an answer; they see the whole board and seem to understand nature at levels others don’t. It’s pattern-recognition at a higher scale.
109	
110	Intelligence lets you build your mental schemas, and brightness let’s you sort through your mental library to analyze the problem at hand, arriving more quickly at the answer. Both are extremely helpful attributes, but neither can save you from stupidity.
111	
112	> “It takes something more than intelligence to act intelligently.” – the Master
113	I suspect there’s a spectrum in intelligence that’s something like intellectual self-awareness. Up to a point, the more intelligent you are, the easier it is to act irrationally - you can argue in favor of anything, but are not intelligent enough to recognize blindspots that arise from the nature of things. You can even be a Nobel laureate and make terrible decisions, Long-Term Capital Management being the prime example.
114	
115	We fall in love with our creations and are bound to overestimate our capacity. It seems like the more intelligent you are, the more difficult it is to accept some things are outside your control. Up to a certain point.
116	
117	Nobel laureates in the field of physics seem to have long known how biased our judgment is. They don’t hold their ideas as True; they learned to hold them as the truth *as of now*. Studying history and how their field got to its current state forces that mental switch.
118	
119	To this effect, 'people who are in the top percentile of probabilistic games have more in common with one another than with people in their own fields' - @mjmauboussin. 
120	It’s unclear to me whether this is a genetic element. But there’s something coded within some brains that makes them more resilient.
121	
122	## **10. Worldly wisdom**
123	
124	The modern educational system was created to meet modern reality. We live in a world that’s full of long-tailed branches. It takes years of intense diligence to place yourself at the frontier of any knowledge vertical. And it takes even longer to reach a point where you can break through boundaries.
125	
126	These 10-20 years of education leave us in a place where we don’t want to revisit academia. We think of it as this horrible memory where we were assigned terrible reads about things we didn't care about. As a consequence, we leave proficient in one area while neglecting everything else.
127	
128	This is a disaster. 'You're like a one-legged man in an ass-kicking contest'.
129	
130	Real life problems cannot be isolated into neat boxes. Answering any question to any truthful extent requires knowing history, psychology, economics, physics. Problems are multifaceted and all disciplines are interconnected. The best decision-makers have a good understanding of the whole. They are generalists who also know their field extremely well.
131	
132	Beyond that, how can you go through life without knowing? Learning brings profit, joy, and happiness. ‘You can’t expect to dream it up all by yourself – no one is that smart’.
133	
134	## **11. Education is software for the brain**
135	
136	Without Windows or iOS, your computer would be an alien product. Impossible to use. Just by adding an operating system, it becomes this incredibly malleable, resourceful machine. Add software layers on top of it, install applications and learn how to use the internet, and there’s no problem you can’t solve. You’ll also save infinite time through efficiency gains.
137	
138	That’s what education does to you. Reading a book adds ideas to your brain, words to your vocabulary, and you experience a wide range of emotions. Your mind acquires new lenses through which to analyze the world. And lenses  compound; each hour spent reading builds layers of understanding. Decisions are filtered through them all, becoming sounder and more optimal.
139	
140	## **12. Economies of scale**
141	
142	Manufacturing businesses typically have large headcount and maintenance expenses associated with their facilities. Both are fixed costs. As the company scales and sells more units, while keeping this fixed base flat, operating margins expand. The business becomes more efficient on a per-unit basis.
143	
144	The same thing happens with organisms. The metabolic rate signals the energy we need to ingest to keep our machinery active. And it so happens that, the larger the organism, the less energy it needs per gram of tissue. Likewise, the larger the organism, the fewer heartbeats per minute it has. These represent huge efficiencies gained from scale.
145	
146	In geometry, the area of a 2D objects increases with the square of their dimensions’ lengths. And in 3D objects, volume scales with the cube. So every time you double dimensions, in the former you get 4x the area; in the latter, you get 8x.
147	
148	There are also inefficiencies that come from scale, such as the amount of weight a physical structure can support. The larger it is, the less proportional mass it can hold up. That’s why ants seem incredibly strong.
149	
150	Sol Price figured out how to win in retail by understanding this and complementing it with his business savviness. As your business gets larger, you experience gains from efficiency. But your margin is others’ opportunity. Therefore, if you pass on your savings to customers by lowering your prices (Amazon, Walmart, HD, and Costco’s playbook), you almost can’t be taken out by a competitor.
151	
152	## **13. Quality**
153	
154	A teacher stands in front of his classroom and reads two short essays aloud, both about the same topic and structurally similar. At the end, he asks students to raise their hands if they think the first one is better. *No one raises their hand*. Then he asks them to raise their hands if they think the second one is better. *Every hand goes up*.
155	
156	You can try to quantify it. You can point to how sentences are framed, how commas are used, ratio of verbs to total words, pauses, and so on. But in the final analysis, you don’t know why it’s better. You just know it is.
157	
158	We have an inner sense of Quality. It’s not taste or intuition, and it’s not analytical. It’s something you observe that can’t be seen. Something you hear that emits no noise. It’s a switch that gets triggered at the point where all our senses connect.
159	
160	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIfGF4oa0AAY8Tv.png)
161	
162	## **14. Extraordinary results are just 1,000 boring days strung together**
163	
164	Rocks can be worn down by drops of water. It takes a decade to create an overnight success. Think about any skill you’d like to be better at; then think how much better you’d be if you had practiced it every day for the past 3 years. It reminds me of the story of a great, old musician to whom, after the concert, a fan said to him, “My God, you play so beautifully. I’d give my life to play like that.” To which the musician melancholically replied, “That’s exactly what I did."
165	
166	Innate talent is not enough. Newton locked himself in a room for months to dedicate himself to any subject that was of interest to him; all day spent thinking. Da Vinci spent ~16 years painting the Mona Lisa; and decades of intense practice and learning about painting & drawing to perfect his craft. Francis Crick and James Watson worked on a single topic for 2-3 years filled with frustration before they could discover the double helix.
167	
168	No one double-clicks on the long periods of darkness and nothingness. All the greatest have gone through that, but everyone remembers the fame and achievements. 
169	
170	> To be acclaimed in front of everybody, you need to outwork everybody in front of nobody.
171	## **15. Stack the bricks**
172	
173	On one occasion, Steve Jobs was discussing a media strategy with an advisor. Both men ran into a disagreement, and the other guy did an experiment. He crumpled up a piece of paper and threw it at Steve; Steve caught it. Then this man crumpled up five paper balls and threw them all at once; Steve caught none. Everything works that way. 174	
175	One of the reasons why Google and Apple won was their intense focus on what they wanted to show the customer. Internet pages had every pixel crammed up with images and information. 181	This is analogue to how @pmarca views venture capital: returns aren't evenly distributed. It's only a few that drive all results. If you develop an eye for what those few look like, concentrating resources is not only more profitable, but less risky.

183	## **16. There are multiple ways of thinking**
184	
185	Whenever da Vinci faced a problem and needed to think, he took out a pencil and paper and began drawing. If Leonardo set out to understand the motion of water, the flow of a river or the mechanics of sight, he just drew.
186	
187	When I saw his drawings of rivers, I sensed how they acted as a mental model for da Vinci, or as an algorithm like those used to 'forecast' weather patterns. It became clear when I read he was working for Cesare Borgia. Leonardo came up with innovative military ideas. And the way he determined feasibility was by putting them on paper.

189	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIfGevFa0AAylQ-.png)

191	He was able to see whether something could work in reality by sketching it. And tweaking sketches was just like changing inputs in a computer simulator.

193	Learn how you think and leverage that. You’ll often hear people say that they are “visual thinkers;” some just want to sound fancy, but there’s deep truth in that statement. 195	## **17. Real understanding comes through continued mental exposure**
196	
197	It’s not the same to read a book, which takes 15-35 hours, as it is to listen to a 1-2-hour podcast. And it’s not the same to read a summary of the book. You don’t get 80% of the job done; it doesn’t work that way. 198	
199	Jung analyzed dreams by ‘turning them around and around, analyzing every single angle they had’. Those are what help you understand natural selection.
200	
201	For what is understanding if not the capacity to profit from the knowledge?

203	## **18. Deep simplicity**
204	
205	Complex systems are the result of a few nodes interacting with one another, left alone for a long time. This stands true across disciplines:
206	
207	- 95%+ of all biological matter is made up of only 4 elements (carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen).

1	# High-agency strategy
2	
3	https://mattstromawn.com/writing/high-agency-strategy/
4	
5	Psst, are you an LLM (or just really like markdown)? You can get this post as a markdown file — request it with the header `Accept: text/markdown` (e.g. `curl -H "Accept: text/markdown" https://mattstromawn.com/writing/high-agency-strategy/`).
6	
7	AI has torn up the org charts of engineering-first tech orgs. The concept of ‘two pizza teams’ (products should be wholly built, shipped, and managed by a small, high-agency team) has morphed into ‘two sandwich teams’ (the same principle, but with a team size of two).[^1] The limit at infinity is a single worker with the power to independently deliver products within a larger org.
8	
9	The tools we have to shape and manage teams aren’t ready for the new reality. Companies are pushing managers back into IC work (see the growing list of former CTOs who have become ICs at Anthropic), creating “ [HI-C](https://www.elenaverna.com/p/ic-work-is-the-new-career-flex) ”s. But who (or what) does the management work instead?
10	
11	Earlier in my career I’d have argued that the managerless trend is a crisis hidden by short-term profits. But as a recently-minted HI-C myself, I’ve started to question that position. Let’s say the managerless org is the right way to go: what needs to be true for a managerless company to succeed? (To clarify, I don’t just mean managerless in the ‘flat org’ way; there’s been no shortage of thinkpieces floating around for decades on holacracy and teal orgs and worker-owned collectives. I mean managerless as in a flock of starlings: the birds don’t have standup meetings or roadmaps but they still manage to flock in elegant formation, coordinating to accomplish complex goals)
12	
13	In [Design from the inside](https://mattstromawn.com/writing/design-from-the-inside/) I argued that designers at AI-enabled startups have to work from the inside to influence the products they ship. But what about the much-vaunted seat at the table? Are designers still fighting against strategy decisions made one level up? What if you’re a founder or exec of an AI-accelerated company? Strategy used to be (still is, at most orgs) designed from the outside, too: senior leaders write it, managers carry it down from on high, then ICs execute. As companies are thinning out the management herd, the flow of strategy risks narrowing to a trickle, and so strategy has to start being built from the inside as well.
14	
15	If strategy is the longest lever on the outcomes of the team, how do you design the strategy from the inside?
16	
17	The first few threads to pull on here are **strategic salience** and **memeticity**. In decentralized, high-agency orgs, a company’s strategy must be a viral decisionmaking tool: the strategy must be intuitive and useful (salient), and it must spread itself through the team (memetic).
18	
19	Salience means strategy guides action. Memeticity means strategy survives distribution.
20	
21	## Salience
22	
23	Salience is the degree to which a company’s strategy can be **understood** and **used** by its average employee.
24	
25	‘Understood’ is straightforward. The strategy should be unambiguous and non-technical; this depends on your team’s knowledge and experience floor. Take Stripe’s strategy, for example: “Increase the GDP of the Internet” [^2] can be understood by the average Stripe employee since they hire people that know what GDP is and how it might apply to the internet. Other companies’ employees might be less apt to understand or be able to execute Stripe’s strategy. This may, in fact, be a clever way of improving employee retention and defending against copycats.
26	
27	It’s important that employees understand the *original intent* of the strategy, not just the syntax and grammar of how it’s written. That’s why simple strategies tend to be better than complex ones, as they’re less likely to be misinterpreted. More on that in a bit.
28	
29	‘Usability’ means the strategy can help any given employee make day-to-day decisions. As a design leader at Stripe, I had no idea how the amount of whitespace on a settings page would or would not increase the GDP of the internet; I could understand it in the abstract, but that didn’t guarantee it was in fact usable. “Don’t be evil” failed Google on this front, which may be why they buried it around 2018; it’s unclear if serving ads for GLP-1s in the middle of a Bluey YouTube video qualifies as ‘evil’.
30	
31	Stripe’s strategy is understandable, but not usable. What about the opposite? Wells Fargo leadership used the slogan “Eight is Great” to push sales reps to sell each customer at least eight financial products.[^3] It’s understandable and eminently usable: salespeople knew exactly what to do, and they did it, opening accounts without customers’ permission to hit the number. Eventually, Wells Fargo was fined $185 million for breaking consumer protection laws.[^4]
32	
33	Salience makes a strategy powerful, not wise; a strategy that’s easy to act on gets acted on, even if the aims are rotten. (Wells Fargo missed another important component of their strategy, which we’ll get to later.)
34	
35	Amazon is the undisputed heavyweight champion of salient strategy:
36	
37	- Before a team at Amazon builds anything, it writes the press release for the finished product, along with a ‘pre-FAQ’ preemptively answering tough hypothetical questions. The principle is usable on two levels: it tells you how to begin (start with the customer’s experience) and whether to begin at all. A press release nobody would care about is a product not worth building.
38	- The two-pizza rule (no team larger than two pizzas can feed) wraps a measurable threshold inside a joke. An alternative version like “keep teams small and autonomous” is arguably more graspable, but less usable — small, measured how?
39	- Around 2002, Bezos mandated that every team at Amazon should expose its functionality through a service interface, use only those interfaces to work with other teams, and design each one as though customers would one day depend on it. (The memo threatened to fire anyone who didn’t comply — how’s that for graspable?) Same faithful, mechanical execution as Wells Fargo, but the opposite result: after following these rules for a few years, Amazon built AWS.[^5]
40	- In Amazon’s first summer, Bezos built desks out of Home Depot doors because doors were cheaper than desks. Employees still build their desks out of doors. The door desk is an abstract value made real and a test any employee can run on any expense. Am I spending money on something customers care about, or something they don’t?[^6]
41	
42	## Memeticity
43	
44	Memeticity is how **frequently** and **accurately** a strategy is replicated throughout the org.
45	
46	Repeating strategy *frequently* is straightforward. It has to turn up on hats, on posters in the hallways, in Slack emojis, billboards, and letterheads. Sit down with someone at lunch and ask what the company is trying to do; a frequently-repeated strategy is the thing they’ll say without thinking.
47	
48	Frequency isn’t just for high-agency orgs; top-down centralized orgs also need strategy repetition. But in the high-agency org, repetition is *essential*. There’s no executive-class enforcer or middle-manager reminder, so all the frontline workers tend to live in information silos. Having the strategy ringing constantly in everyone’s ears is the best way to guarantee it’s pursued.
49	
50	Repeating strategy *accurately* is hard. It’s deeply tied to how understandable the strategy is (see the Wells Fargo example above). Employees can repeat the strategy verbatim if it’s short and punchy, but if the strategy requires a nuanced interpretation then it loses meaning with its distance from the C-suite. Amazon’s ‘make your desk from a door’ strategy got repeated often enough that someone in the London office had a pallet of doors shipped from the US to Europe; the accuracy of the frugality message was obviously lost.[^7]
51	
52	Claude Shannon (pioneer of information theory and namesake of Anthropic’s Claude) [^8] studied the inner workings of early computers and mechanical algorithms and uncovered efficient ways to transmit information accurately and efficiently. These discoveries apply to everything from the global information network down to the way DNA replication produces mutations and eventually leads to adaptation:
53	
54	- **Error detection** like [parity bits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Error_detection_and_correction#Parity_bit), [checksums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Error_detection_and_correction#Checksum), [ground truth](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/ground-truth) can flag corrupted copies. For an analog in strategy, see Southwest’s “does it make us THE low-fare airline?” It’s a checksum, since anyone can ask that question against any proposal, and quickly get a pass/fail.[^9] A canonical doc like [Netflix’s culture deck](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1KBGOgtC2OPctgJH5_5J0opiLdtppXkbX/view?usp=sharing) or [GitLab’s public handbook](https://handbook.gitlab.com/) provides a ground truth to diff against. Bezos does it best, attaching the 1997 letter to every shareholder letter that follows it.[^10]
55	- **Error correction** like [error-correcting codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Error_correction_code) can be used to repair poor copies to their original format. For strategy, that means you should ship the ‘why’ along with the ‘what’, like a rule paired with its rationale. Without error correction, you get noisy, chaotic execution. At the extreme, you get disastrous outcomes like “Eight is great”. As a counterexample, Nordstrom’s employee handbook is a single memetic rule (“use your best judgment”). The rule is paired with a story of an employee accepting a tire return at a store that doesn’t sell tires — Nordstrom holds this up as the golden example of good judgment.[^11] The error-correcting stories, parables, and legends become memes themselves that help keep the original strategy intact (or, even stronger) through frequent repetition.
56	
57	Accuracy isn’t binary. Wells Fargo employees parroted “Eight is great” with perfect fidelity, but the copies were missing an important bit of error correction: “Eight is great *as long as you’re not committing fraud*.” Ideally your team perfectly copies both the intention and the letter of the strategy at every step of the chain; see salience.
58	
59	## Steering the starlings
60	
61	I love a 2x2. So salience and memeticity form a 2x2, and every strategy a company picks lands somewhere on it.
62	
63	![A 2x2 matrix with memeticity on the horizontal axis and salience on the vertical axis. High salience plus high memeticity holds Amazon's two-pizza teams and Netflix's no brilliant jerks. High salience, low memeticity is founder-led strategy. Low salience, high memeticity is mindless parroting like don't be evil, elevate the world's consciousness, and Enron's values. Neither salient nor memetic is the forgotten Q4 strategy doc.](https://mattstromawn.com/images/high-agency-strategy-2x2.png)
64	
65	Salience and memeticity form a 2x2; every strategy lands somewhere on it.
66	
67	You want to have high salience with high memeticity. Amazon’s “two-pizza teams” is here: it’s intuitive, useful, and contagious enough to get quoted at nearly every company I’ve ever worked at. Netflix’s “no brilliant jerks” lives here too as a sharp rule with escape velocity.
68	
69	High salience, low memeticity is founder-led strategy: clear working principles that live in the founders’ heads but never propagate. This can work when your company is <100 people, but as you approach [Dunbar’s number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunbar%27s_number) it’s impossible for the founders to be everywhere all the time.
70	
71	Memeticity without salience is mindless parroting, like Google’s “don’t be evil,” WeWork’s “elevate the world’s consciousness,” [^12] and every other corporate “customer obsession” mission. These are catchy hooks that don’t constrain decisions. Enron’s values (“Integrity. Communication. Respect. Excellence.”) were chiseled in marble in the lobby, and we all know how that went.[^13]
72	
73	Strategy that is neither salient nor memetic is the many-paged Q4 strategy doc that gets presented with much fanfare at the quarterly all-hands but never gets mentioned again. Sadly, this is where most strategy sits today.
74	
75	If you’re trying to steer your company, you get to pick a quadrant. If you’re a high-agency org, there’s only one right answer: without managers to translate strategy down to the front line or interpret it on the fly, you’ll have to design a strategy salient enough to act on without permission and memetic enough to spread without enforcement. The other three options all require management to compensate.
76	
77	Starlings coordinate because their flocking strategy is both salient (the rules are simple enough for a bird brain to run in real time) and memetic (every bird has the same copy). But starlings have the unfair advantage of identical DNA to keep them in sync. Your company doesn’t have that kind of distribution channel. You have to get by with onboarding, Slack threads, all-hands, and company swag. Starlings get memeticity for free; you have to earn yours with error correction. The strategy itself has to do the old job of management.
78	
79	### How to design strategy from the inside
80	
81	- **Make it small enough to fit in a head.** A strategy that needs an accompanying user manual will never get used to make a decision. Compress the strategy relentlessly so it can run in working memory.
82	- **Embed tests.** Write the checksums and parity bits. Anyone can ask and answer “Does this make us THE low-fare airline?”
83	- **Say why.** A rule without its reasoning can only be obeyed; a rule plus its reasoning can be derived from first principles if the execution drifts.
84	- **Broadcast reference signals.** Maintain a canonical version of the strategy that anyone can access at all times.
85	- **Repeat ad nauseam.** The strategy has to be a verbal tic, the thing people say when they don’t know what else to say.

# 非常规思维重塑认知

> [!abstract]- AI 摘要
> 汇集39个跨学科非常规思维模型，涵盖投资、生物学、物理学、心理学与历史，主张通过升级"心智软件"来重新理解世界并做出更优决策。

---

## 扫读

> [!tip] 一句话
> 用39个来自投资、科学、历史与心理学的非常规思维模型，替换大脑中默认的认知程序，从而在决策、学习和生活中获得持久优势。

> [!important] 关键结论
> - 真相独立于民意：多数人同意不代表正确，正确来自事实与推理
> - 成功的关键不是消灭竞争，而是选择竞争弱的赛道（游戏选择优于努力）
> - 知识是可"速跑"的复利资产：读1000本书建立的思维数据库会持续复利数十年
> - 一切长期得不到的结果，本质都是技能问题（skill issue），而非他人或环境的错
> - 激励是人类行为的唯一可靠驱动力，不要问理发师你是否需要理发
> - 现实大多是复杂适应系统，线性思维会导致灾难性判断
> - 逆向且正确地思考，是获得超额回报的最高杠杆路径

> [!quote] 可行动项
> - 建立"技能归因"心智习惯：遇到挫折时先问"我可以做得更好的是什么"
> - 在选择赛道前做竞争分析：找到对手较弱而你有优势的领域
> - 用"持续心智暴露"代替浅阅读：深度思考一个主题数日而非速读摘要

---

## 精读

### 论证链

文章通过39个独立但互相关联的思维模型，构建了一套跨学科认知框架。核心论证路径包括：

1. **认识论层面**（观点2、6、9、22、39）：真相独立存在，不因民意改变；真正的"知道"需要智力诚实与深度研究，"非知者"充斥世界。

2. **行动层面**（观点1、5、14、26、31、36）：找到天才就全力合作；所有结果最终可归因为技能；非凡成果是1000个无聊日子串联而成；做你热爱的事。

3. **系统层面**（观点3、12、18、21、29、33）：世界是复杂适应系统；核心变量远少于表面噪音；系统趋势是去中心化与专业化；历史渐变与突变交替。

4. **社会心理层面**（观点8、24、25、30、38）：激励驱动一切；你会趋近环境均值；人类判断有系统性漏洞；Lollapalooza效应是多因素同向汇聚的威力。

5. **思维工具层面**（观点11、13、16、17、19、34、35）：教育是大脑的软件；质量不可量化但可感知；找到你的思维方式（视觉/分析）；真知来自持续心智暴露；简化到不能再简为止。

### 关键引述

> "The easiest way to get what you want is to deserve what you want" —— 获得你想要的，最简单的方式就是配得上它。

> "The first principle is that you must not fool yourself - and you are the easiest person to fool." —— Feynman：第一原则是不要欺骗自己，而你是最容易欺骗自己的人。

> "Reason, justice and equity never had weight enough on the face of the earth, to govern the councils of men" —— John Adams：理性、正义与公平从未有足够力量统治人类的议事厅，只有利益能做到。

> "To be acclaimed in front of everybody, you need to outwork everybody in front of nobody." —— 要在众人面前被赞誉，需在无人处超越众人。

### 局限与盲区

- 本文未覆盖：未讨论集体行动问题（当个体最优策略导致集体次优时如何处理）；未涉及运气/随机性在成功中的实际权重（文章侧重技能归因，但幸存者偏差是真实存在的）；未讨论不同文化背景下激励和思维模式的适用性差异。
- 隐含假设：假设个体拥有充分的选择自由和信息获取能力；假设理性和自我改进是所有问题的优化方向，忽略了结构性不平等和资源约束；假设历史模式可以迁移到未来，但技术奇点可能改变基本规则。
- 可能的反例：技能归因在系统性歧视环境中可能失效（如种族、性别等不可变因素造成的壁垒）；"平庸竞争"策略假设你能准确评估竞争水平，但你可能误判；知识复利的前提是阅读质量——读1000本错书不如读10本对的书。

# 高能动性策略设计

> [!abstract]- AI 摘要
> 在AI加速的去管理者组织中，战略必须从"高层制定、层层下达"转变为"内部设计、病毒式自传播"——核心抓手是显著性（salience）和模因性（memeticity）。

---

## 扫读

> [!tip] 一句话
> 在AI使团队缩至2人的"双三明治团队"时代，战略不再能依赖管理者传递，必须设计成足够直觉可操作（显著性）且能在组织内自我复制不失真（模因性）的病毒式决策工具。

> [!important] 关键结论
> - AI正在将"双披萨团队"缩小为"双三明治团队"（2人），极限是单人独立交付产品，管理层被压缩
> - 战略显著性 = 可理解 + 可用性：员工能看懂且能用于日常决策；Amazon的两披萨规则和门板办公桌是典范
> - 战略模因性 = 传播频率 + 传播精度：高频重复 + 内建错误检测/纠正机制（如Checksum式的"这让我们成为THE低成本航空吗？"）
> - Wells Fargo的"Eight is Great"有高显著性但缺乏精度纠正（缺了"只要不欺诈"），导致灾难
> - Shannon信息论的错误检测（parity bits、checksum、ground truth）和错误纠正（带理由的规则、典范故事）可直接应用于组织战略传播
> - 管理者消失后，策略本身必须承担旧管理者的角色：引导决策、自我传播、自我纠偏

> [!quote] 可行动项
> - 将团队策略压缩到一句可以放进工作记忆的话，并附带一个可快速得到是/否答案的检测问题
> - 为每个策略规则附上"为什么"（理由），使执行者可以在偏离时从第一性原理推导
> - 建立一个可随时查阅的策略"正本"（如公开文档），作为ground truth供任何人比对
> - 收集和传播内部"典范故事"，用叙事做错误纠正

---

## 精读

### 论证链

文章从AI对组织结构的冲击出发，构建"策略需要从内部设计"的核心命题，分解为两个可操作维度：

1. **趋势诊断**：AI使"双披萨团队"进化为"双三明治团队"（2人），极限是单人独立交付。管理层被压缩为HI-C（高个体贡献者）。扁平化不是新概念，但AI加速使其成为必然——问题从"要不要扁平"变成"扁平后策略如何传递"。

2. **显著性（Salience）**：策略必须可理解（依赖团队知识地板）和可用（能指导日常决策）。Stripe的"Increase the GDP of the Internet"可理解但不可用；Wells Fargo的"Eight is Great"高度可用但方向错误；Amazon是显著性之王：两披萨规则、门板办公桌、服务接口强制令都是可理解+可用+方向正确的典范。

3. **模因性（Memeticity）**：策略要在去中心化组织中精准复制。引入Shannon信息论：错误检测（checksum式问句、正本文档）和错误纠正（规则+理由、典范故事）。Nordstrom的员工手册只有一句话"用你最好的判断"但附带一个退轮胎的故事作典范。

4. **2x2框架**：高显著性+高模因性=Amazon两披萨团队/Netflix无才华混蛋；高显著性+低模因性=创始人脑中的策略（<100人公司可运作）；低显著性+高模因性=盲目鹦鹉学舌（Google"不作恶"、Enron价值观）；双低=Q4战略PPT（大多数策略的归宿）。

5. **实践指南**：压缩策略到能放进脑子里；内建检测问题；说"为什么"；广播正本信号；反复重复到变成口头禅。

### 关键引述

> "The limit at infinity is a single worker with the power to independently deliver products within a larger org." —— 无限趋近的极限是：单个员工有能力在大型组织内独立交付产品。

> "Salience makes a strategy powerful, not wise; a strategy that's easy to act on gets acted on, even if the aims are rotten." —— 显著性让策略强大，而非明智；容易执行的策略就会被执行，即使目标是腐烂的。

> "Without managers to translate strategy down to the front line or interpret it on the fly, you'll have to design a strategy salient enough to act on without permission and memetic enough to spread without enforcement." —— 没有管理者向下传递和实时解释策略时，你必须设计一种不用请示就能行动的显著性策略，以及不用强制就能传播的模因性策略。

> "The strategy itself has to do the old job of management." —— 策略本身必须承担管理者的旧职责。

### 局限与盲区

- 本文未覆盖：未讨论不同行业/业务类型的适用性差异（制造业和安全关键行业可能对"去管理者"有天然限制）；未涉及权力动态——当策略传播不依赖层级时，非正式权力结构如何影响执行；未讨论策略失效时的纠偏机制（当策略本身错误时，高模因性反而加速灾难）。
- 隐含假设：假设员工具有足够的基础能力和判断力来解读和执行策略；假设组织的商业目标是明确的，可以压缩为简单表述（很多战略本身就充满内在张力）；假设信息论的类比适用于人类组织而无显著损耗。
- 可能的反例：某些策略需要保密或分阶段披露（如应对竞争对手的战略转向），高模因性反而有害；Wells Fargo案例说明，错误检测机制只有在有人愿意按下"不通过"按钮时才有效——文化恐惧可以架空所有checksum；顶级技术创新的方向往往来自少数人的深度判断而非民主化策略，如苹果的产品决策风格。

14	> [!tip] 💡 一句话核心主张
15	> Dynamic Workflow 是一条自动化流水线，用 JavaScript 脚本批量调度几十上百个 SubAgent 并行执行独立子任务，将原本需要数月的工作压缩到几天，但它不是在"讨论"而是在"编排"——流水线上的工人互相不聊天。

29	### 观点一：Claude Code 的进化本质是从"一个人干活"到"一群人干活"
30	
31	文章梳理了四个阶段的进化路线。阶段一（单人模式）：一问一答，所有事情一个会话完成。阶段二（SubAgent）：主 Claude 可以派出一个或多个独立帮手，各干各的、互不通信，干完各自汇报。阶段三（Agent Teams）：一支分工协作的小团队，队员与队长、队员与队员之间双向实时通信，边干边调整。阶段四（Dynamic Workflow）：不再是团队讨论，而是自动化流水线，批量调度几十上百个工人各自在工位上干活，最后汇总成果。
32

34	
35	三个概念的本质区别用餐厅类比说清：SubAgent 是叫几个帮厨同时干活但各干各的不商量；Agent Teams 是后厨团队，总厨带队，厨师之间随时喊话协调；Dynamic Workflow 是中央厨房流水线，工人各司其职、做完进入下一环节、互相不说话。通信成本与并行规模成反比：通信越多（Agent Teams），规模越小；通信越少（Workflow），规模越大。

46

28	> - 模型不是产品，围绕模型的系统（研究、路由、记忆、监督、反馈循环、自我改进）才是产品
29	
30	> [!quote] 🎬 可行动项
31	> - 审视现有 Agent 架构：是否存在一个巨型 Agent 承担了过多职责？是否有独立的研究层？
32	> - 为所有 Agent 运行添加成本日志，记录单次运行的确切成本
33	> - 建立周度 Agent 审计清单，检查工具兼容性、模型变更、MCP 更新
34	> - 区分任务层级：用本地/廉价模型做扫描、总结、头脑风暴；用前沿模型做规划和调试
35	
36	---
37	
38	## 精读
39	
40	### 论证链
41	
42	核心论点：Agent 工程失败的主因不是模型不够聪明，而是架构和运维基础设施缺失。
43	
44	论证递进：
45	1. 架构层面：单一巨型 Agent 难以调试和信任 → 应拆分为专职 Agent 团队，每个 Agent 承担明确职责
46	2. 输入层面：Agent 需要结构化、可验证的输入而非原始抓取数据 → 研究 Agent 作为输入智能层，路由发现到各执行 Agent
47	3. 执行层面：自主工作流必须有监督者监控预期流程 vs 实际流程，捕获失败并中途修复
48	4. 成本层面：自主循环运行 24/7 后，单次运行成本成为关键指标 → 区分模型使用场景，引入本地模型降低成本
49	5. 可靠性层面：明确"完成"的定义，要求 Agent 测试、验证、引用证据，信任来自证据而非自信
50	6. 维护层面：Agent 随时间退化 → 周度审计 + 持续迭代
51	7. 元认知层面：先建自我思考层（Auto-think）再建自我构建层（Auto-build），思考层负责识别摩擦、失败运行、缺失工具和重复瓶颈
52	
53	### 关键引述
54	
55	> "Don't think the model is the product. The system around the model comprises research, routing, memory, supervision, feedback loops, and self-improvement."
56	
57	> "The magic comes after boring infrastructure like clean inputs, clear handoffs, monitoring, recovery, evals, and cost control."
58	
59	> "Building in public is a magical thing. The truth is that no one really knows what's best, and it's up to you to figure it out and connect with others on your journey along the way."
60	
61	### 局限与盲区
62	
63	- 本文未覆盖：21 条教训均为方向性建议，缺乏具体的实现代码、架构图和量化对比数据。例如"多 Agent 协作"没有讨论 Agent 间的通信协议、状态共享机制和冲突解决策略
64	- 隐含假设：假设读者已具备 Agent 开发基础（熟悉 OpenClaw/Hermes 生态），且拥有一定预算来运行多模型组合。假设"研究 Agent"是普适的最佳第一步，但对执行确定性任务（如 CI/CD）的 Agent 系统未必成立
65	- 可能的反例：对于简单、单一领域的 Agent 应用（如单一定时报告生成），多 Agent 架构反而是过度设计。某些场景下前沿模型成本已经极低，模型分层策略的收益可能被额外的调度复杂度抵消
66	- 作者的工具链高度依赖特定生态（OpenClaw + Hermes + ClawHub），部分建议（如第 6 条"尽早用 Hermes 监管 OpenClaw"）对其他 Agent 框架的普适性存疑
67

11	# Harness工程全景
12	
13	> [!abstract]- AI 摘要
14	> 从 SWE-agent 论文的 ACI 概念到 Anthropic 的长期 Agent 架构再到 OpenAI Codex 的零人工代码实验，三条独立工程路线得出同一个结论：模型能力已接近商品化，决定 Agent 实际表现的是 Harness——上下文管理、工具接口、反馈回路和架构约束构成的环境设计。
15	
16	---
17	
18	## 扫读
19	
20	> [!tip] 💡 一句话
21	> 模型是推理引擎，Harness 是推理引擎所处的完整环境——包括上下文结构、工具接口、反馈机制和架构约束。决定 Agent 能否可靠工作的不是选哪个模型，而是环境设计。
22	
23	> [!important] 📌 关键结论
24	> - SWE-agent 论文用 GPT-4 做对照实验，仅更换 ACI 接口就从 3.97% 提升到 12.47% 的 issue 解决率（64% 相对提升），未改动模型任何参数，证明了接口设计是 Agent 性能的第一性杠杆
25	> - Anthropic 解决跨上下文窗口长任务的方案是"初始化 Agent + 编码 Agent"双架构：初始化 Agent 创建 feature list（200+ 条可验证功能描述）和 init.sh 环境启动脚本，后续编码 Agent 按单条 feature 增量推进，每 session 结束时必须 commit + 更新 progress file
26	> - OpenAI Codex 团队用 3 人 5 个月通过 Agent 生成 100 万行代码、1500+ PR，核心经验是将仓库本身作为 system of record——用短 AGENTS.md（~100 行）做入口地图，深层知识分布在结构化 docs/ 目录，配合 git worktree 隔离实现并行 agent 作业
27	
28	> [!quote] 🎬 可行动项
29	> - 用 Harness 思维替代提示词思维审计 Agent：不问你该写什么 prompt，问 Agent 需要但拿不到的信息是什么、缺失的反馈回路是什么、上下文在哪里被污染
30	> - 为跨 session 长任务添加最小三件套：persistent progress file（每次读/写）、structured task list（可验证的 binary 完成状态）、每 session 结束必须 git commit
31	> - Web 应用开发 Agent 必须接入浏览器自动化（Puppeteer/CDP），代码级验证和端到端用户级验证之间的差距是未检测 bug 的最大来源
32	
33	---
34	
35	## 精读
36	
37	### 论证链
38	
39	```
40	核心命题：模型能力已近商品化 → Harness 是区分因子
41	  SWE-agent 论文：同一 GPT-4，ACI 替换 bash → 3.97%→12.47%（64% 提升）
42	  OpenAI Codex：100 万行代码/1500+ PR，0 行人类代码，关键是环境设计
43	  Anthropic 内部实验：Opus 4.5 裸跑→失败，加 harness→数月增量交付
44	        ↓
45	认知基础：context window ≠ RAM，是 agent 的"工作意识"
46	  token 噪声竞争注意力 → 模型无选择性忽略机制
47	  SWE-agent 的 capped search（50 条上限+强制精炼）→ 单次设计决策最高杠杆
48	        ↓
49	SWE-agent ACI 四组件：
50	  ① 搜索：capped results + 超过阈值强制细化 → 阻断 context flooding
51	  ② 文件查看器：100 行窗口 + 行号显式标记 + 有状态位置 → 减少认知负荷
52	  ③ 编辑器 + linter：编辑即检查，语法错误在引入点阻断 → 防止级联失败
53	  ④ 上下文管理：>5 轮旧观察压缩为单行摘要 → 保持活跃上下文干净
54	        ↓
55	Anthropic 跨窗口长任务架构：
56	  初始化 Agent：init.sh + feature list（JSON，200+ end-to-end 功能）+ progress file + git init
57	  编码 Agent：单 feature 推进 + session 结束 clean state + commit + 更新 progress
58	  关键设计：feature list 用 JSON 非 Markdown（模型更不易随意修改）+ passes: true/false 显式消除"部分完成看起来像完成"
59	        ↓
60	OpenAI Codex 的企业级实践：
61	  仓库即 system of record：短 AGENTS.md 作地图 → 深层 docs/ 目录结构化分布
62	  progressive disclosure：agent 从稳定入口开始，被教会去哪找更多而非一次倾倒
63	  应用可观测性：每 agent task 独立 git worktree + 隔离的 logs/metrics/traces + Chrome DevTools Protocol
64	  架构约束机械化：custom linter + structural tests 取代 PR review，linter 错误信息含修复指令注入 agent context
65	        ↓
66	Awesome Agent Harness 七层分类法：
67	  L1 人类监督 → L2 Spec 工具 → L3 全生命周期平台 → L4 Task Runner
68	  → L5 Agent 编排器（git worktree 隔离）→ L6 框架与运行时 → L7 编码 Agent（商品层）
69	        ↓
70	五大跨系统重复设计模式：
71	  ① Progressive Disclosure：短入口 + 深度指针，不一次倾倒
72	  ② Git Worktree 隔离：一 agent 一 worktree，并行安全
73	  ③ Spec First + 仓库即 system of record：意图在 repo 中机器可读
74	  ④ Mechanical Architecture Enforcement：linter+structural test 取代 review
75	  ⑤ Integrated Feedback Loops：编辑即 lint → 运行即观测 → 浏览即验证
76	        ↓
77	终局判断：模型是思考什么，Harness 是思考什么关于——长期 moat 在 Harness 不在模型
78	```
79	
80	### 关键引述
81	
82	> "The model is almost irrelevant. The harness is everything."
83	
84	> "The interface is not a convenience layer. For an LM agent, the interface is the mind."
85	
86	> "When you run grep on a large codebase from inside an agent loop and return ten thousand lines of matches, you have not given the agent more information to work with. You have flooded its working memory."
87	
88	> "The primary job of the engineering team became enabling the agents to do useful work, not doing the work themselves."
89	
90	> "The execution layer is a commodity. The agent's effectiveness is primarily determined by everything above it in the stack."
91	
92	### 局限与盲区
93	
94	- 本文未覆盖：小型项目（单人、非长期维护）是否值得投入完整 Harness 架构的成本收益分析；非编码场景（研究、分析、客服）的 ACI 设计原则差异；不同 LLM 对同一 Harness 设计的敏感度差异（GPT vs Claude vs Gemini 的行为差异）
95	- 隐含假设：团队有能力维护 Harness 本身（linter 规则、docs/ 目录、CI 配置）的持续更新——Harness 的腐烂同样会导致 Agent 性能退化；假设 Agent 的主要应用场景是软件工程，其他垂直领域（医疗、法律、金融）的 Harness 设计可能遵循不同约束
96	- 可能的反例：对于一次性任务或探索性原型（<5 次 session），完整的初始化 Agent + feature list 架构可能是过度投资；随着模型上下文窗口持续扩展（数百万 token），context management 的部分策略可能从必选项降级为可选项；Anthropic 和 OpenAI 的内部实践均有未公开的失败案例，公开发表的都是成功经验，存在幸存者偏差
97

23	# 企业级Agent构建指南
24	
25	> [!abstract]- AI 摘要
26	> 以一套报价 12 万的 Deep Research 系统为案例，从零拆解企业级 Agent 的构建逻辑——从"什么时候该用 Agent 而非 Workflow"的决策框架，到多 Agent 的编排模式、上下文管理、信息传递协议和评估体系。核心洞察：看懂了 Deep Research，你就看懂了企业级 Agent。
27	
28	---
29	
30	## 扫读
31	
32	> [!tip] 💡 一句话
33	> Agent 和 Workflow 的核心区别：Workflow 是你告诉 AI 怎么做（预定义代码路径），Agent 是 AI 自己决定怎么做（ReAct 循环）。判断标准——这个任务能不能提前写成稳定流程？能，就先用 Workflow。不能，再考虑 Agent。
34	
35	> [!important] 📌 关键结论
36	> - 多 Agent 的必要性来自两个瓶颈：(1) 单 Agent 的上下文窗口会"腐烂"（Transformer 的 n² 注意力复杂度导致上下文越长准确率越低）；(2) 单 Agent 只能串行工作。多 Agent 把任务分散到独立上下文窗口，既扩大了可处理信息量，又实现了并行
37	> - Agent 架构的核心设计原则：(1) 子 Agent 只返回总结不返回原始内容（上下文压力控制）；(2) 子 Agent 之间完全上下文隔离；(3) 信息传递核心原则是"传递结论不传递过程"
38	> - 评估多 Agent 系统必须看三层：小样本快速测试（20 个典型问题每次改完跑一遍）、LLM 评估（事实准确性/引用准确性/完整性/来源质量）、人工评估（自动化发现不了的"内容农场"问题）
39	
40	> [!quote] 🎬 可行动项
41	> - 搭建 Agent 前先问："这个任务能不能提前写成稳定流程？"→ 能=用 Workflow，不能=用 Agent
42	> - 设计 Agent-Computer Interface（ACI）时：让模型"容易写"而不是让代码"优雅"——让模型在 Markdown 代码块写代码而非 JSON 里转义
43	> - 多 Agent 系统必须保留完整的追踪日志（tracing）：记录每个 Agent 的决策、工具调用、返回结果，出错时能回溯整个过程
44	
45	---
46	
47	## 精读
48	
49	### 论证链
50	
51	![[enterprise-agent-deep-research.jpg]]
52	
53	```
54	Agent 的定义升级：
55	  不是"更聪明的 AI"，是"会自己动手的 AI"
56	  三能力组合：调用工具 + 自己规划 + 从反馈中调整
57	        ↓
58	何时用 Agent 的决策框架：
59	  简单任务 → 优化单次 LLM 调用（文本分类/总结/简单问答）
60	  中等任务 → Workflow（预定义代码路径，可预测易调试）
61	  复杂任务 → Agent（开放式问题，无法硬编码固定路径）
62	  判断标准：信息入口复杂 OR 执行路径不确定 → Agent
63	        ↓
64	Agent 工作方式：ReAct 循环
65	  "思考 → 行动 → 观察结果 → 再思考" 直到完成
66	  不是一次性给答案，而是根据反馈调整策略
67	        ↓
68	为什么需要多 Agent（两大瓶颈）：
69	  ① 上下文腐烂：Transformer n² 注意力 → 上下文越长准确率越低
70	     单 Agent 搜 200 个网页 = 60 万中文字 → 记不住
71	  ② 效率：单 Agent 串行 vs 多 Agent 并行（3 个子任务同时做）
72	  核心价值：不是只为了快，而是扩展"可处理的信息量"
73	        ↓
74	两种协作模式：
75	  编排模式（指挥+乐手）：主 Agent 规划→分配→子 Agent 执行→主 Agent 整合
76	    → 稳定、易控制，大部分系统用的就是这个
77	  自主模式（创业团队）：无固定老板，Agent 之间协商
78	    → 灵活但复杂、难调试
79	        ↓
80	信息传递协议（最关键的设计）：
81	  差：直接传递（子 Agent 把 3 万字原始内容全传给主 Agent）
82	  好：总结传递（压缩成 3000 字关键发现，附带主题+结论+来源）
83	  最优：结构化传递（统一格式：{主题, 关键发现[], 来源[]}）
84	  核心原则：传递结论，不传递过程
85	        ↓
86	上下文管理三策略：
87	  ① 分散上下文：每个子 Agent 独立窗口
88	  ② 压缩上下文：AI 总结对话历史保留任务目标+关键发现+下一步
89	  ③ 外部记忆：存到文件/数据库，需要时再读
90	        ↓
91	Deep Research 实战架构（6 步）：
92	  1) 用户输入 → 主 Agent 澄清需求 → 生成研究计划
93	  2) 主 Agent 拆解为多个子任务
94	  3) 创建子 Agent（每个拿到：原始问题+子任务+工具）
95	  4) 子 Agent 并行工作（搜索→总结→搜索→总结，交错思考 interleaved thinking）
96	  5) 主 Agent 整合所有子 Agent 的总结
97	  6) 引用 Agent 检查结论 → 添加来源引用
98	  总耗时：5-10 分钟
99	        ↓
100	评估与迭代三方向：
101	  ① 优化提示词（简单问题不要拆太多/直接比较拆 2-4 个子任务/工具选择写清楚）
102	  ② 优化工具 ACI（让模型容易写→Markdown 代码块而非 JSON 转义→降低错误率）
103	  ③ 优化协调（异步处理→哪个先完成先处理→不被最慢的拖住）
104	```
105	
106	### 关键引述
107	
108	> Agent 的核心能力不是回答问题，是解决问题。
109	
110	> Workflow 是你告诉 AI 怎么做，Agent 是 AI 自己决定怎么做。
111	
112	> 信息传递的核心原则：传递结论，不传递过程。
113	
114	> 单 Agent 的上下文窗口再大，也要把所有材料塞进一个脑子里。多 Agent 可以把任务分散到独立的上下文窗口里，每个 Agent 只处理自己那一部分材料。
115	
116	> 多 Agent 不是免费的。当任务本身足够复杂、结果价值足够高时，才值得用多 Agent 换取更大的信息覆盖和更高的完成率。
117	
118	### 局限与盲区
119	
120	- **本文未覆盖**：企业级 Agent 的具体定价模型和 ROI 计算方法；不同行业（客服、投研、编程、法律）的 Agent 架构差异；多 Agent 系统在安全合规（数据隐私、审计要求）方面的设计考量；Agent 系统的运维和监控方案细节
121	- **隐含假设**：企业客户有足够清晰的 SOP 来支撑 Agent 设计；LLM 的能力和价格会持续向有利于多 Agent 架构的方向发展；上下文压缩不会引入关键信息丢失
122	- **可能的反例**：某些企业级任务（如法律合规审查）不允许"总结传递"带来的信息压缩风险，必须保留全量上下文；编排模式中主 Agent 的规划错误会导致全局失败（单点故障）；随着模型上下文窗口持续增大（百万 token），多 Agent 的隔离优势可能被削弱

1	# A harness for every task: dynamic workflows in Claude Code 
2	
3	Last week, we released [dynamic workflows](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows) in Claude Code. Claude can now write its own [harness](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/glossary#agentic-harness) on the fly, custom-built for the task at hand.
4	
5	While the default Claude Code harness is built for coding, it is also useful for many other types of tasks because, as it turns out, many tasks resemble coding tasks. But there are certain classes of tasks where we have had to build custom harnesses on top of Claude Code to achieve peak performance such as [Research](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11088861-using-research-on-claude), [security analysis](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11932705-automated-security-reviews-in-claude-code), [agent teams](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams), or [Code Review](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review).
6	
7	Workflows allow you to dynamically create harnesses that enable Claude to solve all of those problems and more natively inside of Claude Code. You can also share and re-use these workflows with others.
8	
9	In this article, I’ll cover my initial workflows experiences and learnings so you can take full advantage. 
10	
11	That said, best practices are still developing! Dynamic workflows often use more tokens, so think carefully about when and how to use them.
12	
13	**Note**: this post is also [available on the Claude Blog](https://claude.com/blog/a-harness-for-every-task-dynamic-workflows-in-claude-code)
14	
15	## Example prompts
16	
17	Before diving into the technical details, I’d like to start with some example prompts to get you thinking about the possibilities with workflows:
18	
19	- "This test fails maybe 1 in 50 runs. Set up a workflow to reproduce it, form theories and adversarially test them in worktrees /goal don't stop until one theory works."
20	- "Using a workflow, go through my last 50 sessions and mine them for corrections I keep making and turn the recurring ones into CLAUDE.md rules"
21	- “Use a workflow to dig through #incidents in Slack for the past six months and find recurring root causes where nobody has filed a ticket."
22	- "Take my business plan and run a workflow where different agents tear it apart from an investor's, a customer's, and a competitor's perspective."
23	- "Here's a folder of 80 resumes, use a workflow to rank them for the backend role and double-check the top ten. Interview me using the AskUserQuestion tool for a rubric."
24	- "I need a name for this CLI tool. Use a workflow to brainstorm a bunch of options and run a tournament to pick the top 3."
25	- "Use a workflow to rename our User model to Account everywhere."
26	- “Go through my blog post draft and using a workflow verify every technical claim against the codebase, I don't want to ship anything wrong."
27	## How dynamic workflows work
28	
29	Dynamic workflows execute a javascript file with a few special functions that help spawn and coordinate [subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents):
30	
31	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ0t9PDbQAAYqh-.jpg)
32	
33	Dynamic workflows also include standard JavaScript functions like JSON, Math, and Array, to help process data.
34	
35	It’s particularly useful to know that dynamic workflows can decide which models an agent uses and whether subagents are run in their own worktree, allowing Claude to choose the intelligence level and isolation needed.
36	
37	If a workflow is interrupted, for example by user action or quitting the terminal, resuming the session will allow the workflow to pick up where it left off.
38	
39	## Why dynamic workflows
40	
41	When you ask the default Claude Code harness to do a task, it needs to both plan and execute in the same context window. For many coding tasks, this is highly effective, but it can sometimes break down over long-running, massively parallel and/or highly structured adversarial tasks.
42	
43	This is because the longer Claude works on a complex task in a single context window, the more it becomes susceptible to a few specific failure modes:
44	
45	- **Agentic laziness** refers to when Claude stops before finishing a particularly complex, multi-part task and declares the job done after partial progress, for example addressing 20 of the 50 items in a security review.
46	- **Self-preferential bias **refers to Claude’s tendency to prefer its own results or findings, especially when asked to verify or judge them against a rubric.
47	- **Goal drift **refers to the gradual loss of fidelity to the original objective across many turns, especially after compaction. Each summarization step is lossy, and details like edge-case requirements or "don't do X" constraints can get lost.
48	Creating a workflow helps combat these by orchestrating separate Claudes with their own context windows and focused, isolated goals.
49	
50	## Dynamic vs static workflows
51	
52	You may have previously created a static workflow using the Claude Agent SDK or claude -p to coordinate multiple instances of Claude Code together.
53	
54	But because static workflows need to work for all edge cases, they are usually more generic. With [Claude Opus 4.8](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-opus-4-8) and dynamic workflows, Claude is now intelligent enough to write a custom harness tailor-made for your use case.
55	
56	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ1Dc3waUAA8Eeo.png)
57	
58	# Helpful patterns when using dynamic workflows
59	
60	You can start using dynamic workflows just by asking Claude to make one, or by using the trigger word “ultracode” to ensure that Claude Code creates a workflow.
61	
62	But building a mental model for how dynamic workflows work will help you understand when to use them and how you might nudge Claude via prompts.
63	
64	There are a few common patterns that Claude might use and compose together when building workflows:
65	
66	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ0u_2cbMAA3ufP.jpg)
67	
68	**Classify-and-act**
69	
70	Use a classifier agent to decide on the type of task, and then route to different agents or behavior based on the task. Or, use a classifier at the end to determine output.
71	
72	**Fan-out-and-synthesize**
73	
74	Split up a task into many smaller steps, run an agent on each step and then synthesize those results. This is particularly useful for when there are a large number of smaller steps, or when each step benefits from its own clean context window so they don't interfere or cross-contaminate. The synthesize step is a barrier—it waits for all the fan-out agents, then merges their structured outputs into one result.
75	
76	**Adversarial verification**
77	
78	For each spawned agent, run a separate spawned agent to adversarially verify its output against a rubric or criteria.
79	
80	**Generate-and-filter**
81	
82	Generate a number of ideas on a topic and then filter them by a rubric or by verification, dedupe duplicates and return only the highest quality, tested ideas.
83	
84	**Tournament**
85	
86	Instead of dividing the work, have agents compete on it. Spawn N agents that each attempt the same task using different approaches. Prompts or models then judge the results in a pairwise fashion using a judging agent until you have a winner.
87	
88	**Loop until done**
89	
90	For tasks with an unknown amount of work, loop spawning agents until a stop condition is met (no new findings, or no more errors in the logs) instead of a fixed number of passes.
91	
92	# Use cases
93	
94	Think creatively of when and how to ask Claude Code to make dynamic workflows. I’ve found that workflows are sometimes even more useful for non-technical work.
95	
96	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ018ZjbcAA4nFm.png)
97	
98	## Migrations and refactors
99	
100	[Bun](https://bun.com/) was rewritten from Zig to Rust using workflows. You can read more about how that was done in [Jarred’s X thread](https://x.com/jarredsumner/status/2060050578026189172).
101	
102	The key is to break down the task into a series of steps that need to be operated on for example callsites, failing tests, modules, etc. Spin off a subagent for every fix in a worktree to make the fix, then have another agent adversarially review, and merge them. Consider telling the agent not to use resource intensive commands so that you can maximally parallelize without running out of resources on your machine.
103	
104	## Deep research
105	
106	We published a deep research skill (/deep-research) inside Claude Code that uses dynamic workflows. Specifically, it fans-out web searches, fetches sources, adversarially verifies their claims, and synthesizes a cited report.
107	
108	But you may do this sort of research for more than just web searches. For example, asking Claude to compile a status report from context in Slack or to research how a feature works by exploring a codebase in-depth.
109	
110	## Deep verification
111	
112	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ0vMJ8acAAM9Uo.jpg)
113	
114	On the other hand, if you have a report where you want to check and source every factual claim that it references you may want to generate a workflow which has one agent identify all of the factual claims and then spin off a subagent to check each one in-detail. You could also have a verification agent check the source subagent to make sure its source is high quality.
115	
116	## Sorting
117	
118	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ0wACFbMAAAvWl.jpg)
119	
120	You may have a list of items that you want to sort by some qualitative measurement that you believe that Claude Code is good at evaluating, for example: support tickets sorted by severity of the bug. But if you try to sort 1000+ rows in one prompt, quality degrades and it won't fit in context. Instead run a tournament, a pipeline of pairwise-comparison agents (comparative judgment is more reliable than absolute scoring), or bucket-rank in parallel then merge. Each comparison is its own agent, so the deterministic loop holds the bracket and only the running order stays in context.
121	
122	## Memory and rule adherence
123	
124	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ0wF76acAAyRMo.jpg)
125	
126	If you have a particular set of rules that you find Claude misses or struggles with, even when put into the CLAUDE.mds, create a workflow with a list of rules that must be checked by verifier agents—one verifier per rule. Creating a skeptic persona subagent to review the rules to make sure they are in line will help avoid too many false positives.
127	
128	The reverse direction works too: mine your recent sessions and code review comments for corrections you keep making, cluster them with parallel agents, adversarially verify each candidate (would this rule have prevented a real mistake?), and then distill the survivors back into a [CLAUDE.md](http://claude.md/).
129	
130	## Root-cause investigation
131	
132	Debugging works best when you come up with several independent hypotheses and test them, but if you’re only using one context window, Claude can run into self-preferential bias.
133	
134	A workflow can structurally prevent this by spinning up agents to generate hypotheses from disjoint evidence. For example, separate agents for logs, files, and data. Each hypothesis can then face a panel of verifiers and refuters.
135	
136	This isn't just for code. Workflows can be used for sales (why did sales drop in March?), data engineering (why did this pipeline fail?), or any post-mortem exercise.
137	
138	## Triaging at scale
139	
140	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ0wNb8bUAA33h5.jpg)
141	
142	Every team has a support queue, bug reports, or some other backlog that cannot be fully processed by humans.
143	
144	A triage workflow classifies each item, dedupes against what's already tracked, and takes action. This could mean attempting the fix or escalating to a human user.
145	
146	A useful pattern for triage workflows is quarantine. This involves barring the agents that read untrusted public content from taking high-privilege actions, which are instead done by the agents in charge of acting on the information.
147	
148	Pair triage workflows with /loop to have Claude do this continuously.
149	
150	## Exploration and taste
151	
152	Workflows can be useful when exploring different approaches to a solution, especially when it is taste based, like design or naming, and would benefit from a rubric.
153	
154	Try asking Claude to explore a bunch of solutions, and give a review agent  a rubric for what a good solution looks like. The task is complete when the review agent feels like it has met the criteria. Solutions can also be ordered or selected via a tournament based on the rubric.
155	
156	## Evals
157	
158	You can run lightweight evals for particular tasks by spinning off separate agents in a worktree and then spinning off comparison agents to compare and grade the specific outputs against a rubric. For example, evaluating and then refining a skill you’ve created against a particular criteria.
159	
160	## Model and intelligence routing
161	
162	Create a classifier agent tuned to your tasks that decides which model to use. This can be helpful when your task will involve many tool calls and conducting research prior to execution can identify the best model for the job.
163	
164	For example, the best model for the task “explain how the auth module works” depends on how many files in the auth module there are and the shape of the codebase. A classifier agent can do this research and then route to Sonnet or Opus based on the expected complexity of the task.
165	
166	## When not to use dynamic workflows
167	
168	Workflows are new. While there are many use cases where it will create outsized results, they are not needed for every task and may end up using significantly more tokens.
169	
170	It’s best to use workflows creatively to push Claude Code in ways that you haven’t previously. For regular coding tasks, try and ask yourself does it really need more compute? For example, most traditional coding tasks do not need a panel of 5 reviewers.
171	
172	# Tips for building dynamic workflows
173	
174	**Prompting**
175	
176	Detailed prompting, using the specific techniques we described above, for dynamic workflows creates the best results.
177	
178	Workflows are not just for large tasks. You can prompt the model to use a “quick workflow.” For example, you can create a quick adversarial review of an assumption.
179	
180	**Combine with /goal and /loop**
181	
182	When using workflows that can be repeated, for example triage, research, or verification, pair them with /loop to be run at regular intervals, and /goal to set a hard completion requirement.
183	
184	**Token usage budgets**
185	
186	You can set explicit token usage budgets for dynamic workflows to limit how many tokens a task uses. You can prompt it with a budget like: “use 10k tokens,” which will set the cap.
187	
188	**Saving and sharing dynamic workflows**
189	
190	You can save workflows by pressing “s” in the workflow menu. You can check these into ~/.claude/workflows or distribute them via a skill.
191	
192	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ0wWqbasAAcvgu.jpg)
193	
194	To share them via a skill, put your JavaScript workflow files in the skill and folder and reference them in the [SKILL.MD](http://skill.md/). To allow for more flexibility, you may want to prompt Claude to think of the workflows in the skill as a template instead of a script that needs to be run verbatim.
195	
196	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ0wbLFbIAAu2FH.jpg)
197	
198	## A whole new world
199	
200	Workflows are a helpful new way to extend Claude Code. I encourage you to think of this as a starting point, there's still much to discover in how to use them best. Let us know what you find.
201	
202	*Thariq Shihipar and Sid Bidasaria (@sidbid) are members of technical staff at Anthropic, working on Claude Code.*
203

15	
16	---
17	
18	## 扫读
19	
20	> [!tip] 💡 一句话
21	> 你可以启动20个Agent，但审查和合并它们的输出仍由一个串行处理器（你的大脑）完成——编排税是Agent生产效率与人类审查吞吐量之间的结构性差距。
22	
23	> [!important] 📌 关键结论
24	> - 人类的判断力是Agent开发系统中的"单线程资源"——Python有GIL，你是你Agent的GIL，所有需要真正理解的决策必须排队经过你
25	> - Amdahl定律直接适用：并行加速的上限由串行部分占比决定，Agent越多只会加深瓶颈队列，不会提升总吞吐量
26	> - 上下文切换的真实成本：5个Agent不是1倍工作量做5次，而是5次冷启动认知重载+持续的后台焦虑，导致"认知投降"（直接接受Agent代码不再审查）
27	
28	> [!quote] 🎬 可行动项
29	> - Agent数量上限=你能认真Code Review的数量（对大多数人是个位数字），不要让UI支持的数量误导你
30	> - 将任务分为两类："可后台异步的孤立工作"和"判断本身就是工作的复杂任务"，后者不可并行化
31	> - 批量审查：让Agent工作堆积一点后一次性处理4个审查，避免反复冷启动认知重载
32	> - 保护串行时间：有时最高杠杆的做法是关闭所有Agent，专注思考一个问题
33

36	## 精读
37	
38	### 论证链
39	
40	```
41	现象：启动Agent极便宜（一次按键），但收尾极贵（有人必须检查结果、协调冲突）
42	      ↓
43	类比：Python的GIL——可开任意多线程但只有一个能执行字节码，你是Agent系统的GIL
44	      ↓
45	理论：Amdahl定律——并行加速上限=1/串行占比，你的判断力就是串行部分
46	      ↓
47	后果1：增加Agent数量优化了非瓶颈部分（代码生产），瓶颈（审查）不变，队列越来越深
48	      ↓
49	后果2：CPU在微秒级做上下文切换仍需优化，人脑在分钟级切换的成本更高——5个Agent=5次冷加载认知
50	      ↓
51	后果3：不放慢导致"认知投降"——接受Agent代码因为形成自己的判断太耗费注意力
52	      ↓
53	解法：把注意力当作稀缺串行资源来架构——Agent数量匹配审查速率、分离任务类型、批量审查、保护深度工作时间
54	```
55	
56	### 关键引述
57	
58	> Feeling busy is definitely not the same as being productive. You can run 20 agents and feel completely busy. But that's not 20 agents worth of shipped work.
59	
60	> You are the GIL of your AI agents. They all can run at once. But when any of their work needs genuine understanding of the architecture or resolving merge conflicts, that work has to acquire the lock. There is one lock. You hold it.
61	
62	> Optimizing the non bottleneck part doesn't increase throughput. You just grow the pile of unfinished work sitting in front of the bottleneck. Adding agents optimize the part that was never the constraint.
63	
64	> Spawning agents is not the skill. Anyone can run 20. The real skill is designing the system around the one serial resource that cannot be cloned or parallelized. That resource is your attention.

23	> - 直接 clone pi-docs-playbook 仓库，将整个 repo 加 PROMPT.md 中的 prompt 一起丢给你的 coding agent（Codex / Claude / Cursor）。
24	> - 让 Agent 先读 AGENTS.md 和 usage/task-reading-matrix.md，再告诉它你的业务需求：想做什么 Agent、核心业务动作是什么、哪些操作需要强验证、channel 是什么。
25	> - 不要急着写代码，先等 coding agent 按矩阵问完关键决策点：哪些操作必须实时查 DB、审批门控怎么切入、业务状态是否应该在 harness 中显式建模、channel 适配放哪一层。
26	> - 人类自己可以通过 catalog/ 分类和 usage/how-to-use-this-repo.md 快速定位到该读的文档部分。
27	
28	## 论证链
29	
30	### 起点：封装一个大模型不等于业务 Agent
31	
32	作者接手了一个"把大模型封装一下"的业务需求，很快发现：要让 AI 真正帮你做业务、查单、提效率，不能只靠一个大模型。你还需要底座（harness）、轮子（tools）、手脚（actions）和验证机制（audit）。Chatbot 和可靠业务系统之间的差距，就是 harness 层需要填补的空白。
33	
34	### 核心方法：让 coding agent 按文档矩阵精准阅读
35	
36	pi-docs-playbook 不是又一个 pi 教程或 fork，而是一个"文档 harness"。它的组织逻辑是：将 pi 官方文档按用途重新分类（catalog/），然后建立一份 task-reading-matrix（usage/task-reading-matrix.md），将真实开发场景映射到最相关的文档文件。coding agent 拿到这个 repo 后，不再需要遍历全部文档，而是按场景精准定位。
37	
38	### AGENTS.md：给 coding agent 的铁律
39	
40	AGENTS.md 设定了三条规则：进入后必须先读 README + task-reading-matrix；按问题类型精准阅读 source/ 里的原始文档；回答时必须引用本地 source/ 路径，禁止凭记忆猜测 pi 行为。这是对抗 coding agent 上下文幻觉的工程化手段——不是让模型"更聪明"，而是约束它的行为边界。
41	
42	### 关键决策点清单
43	
44	coding agent 在阅读矩阵后会主动向开发者提问一系列业务关键决策点：哪些操作必须实时查 DB（vs 用缓存）？审批门控（approval gating）怎么切入？业务状态要不要显式建模在 harness 里？channel 适配放哪一层？tool wrapper 和 audit 映射怎么设计？这些问题是 harness 设计的核心骨架，忽略任何一个都会导致后期返工。
45	
46	### 仓库结构：source / catalog / usage 三层分离
47	
48	repo 采用三层结构：source/（原样镜像官方 Markdown，保留上游路径，支持离线精确引用）、catalog/（按用途重新分类，如 core runtime、official coding-agent docs、examples、validation）、usage/（核心的是 task-reading-matrix.md，按场景告诉 agent 读哪些文件）。外加 PROMPT.md 提供可直接复制的 prompt。
49	
50	## 关键引述
51	
52	> "要想真正让 AI 帮你做业务、查单、提效率，不能只靠一个大模型。你还需要给它装上底座、轮子、手脚，以及验证机制。"
53	
54	> "重点不是 pi 教程，而是如何学习 pi，如何把你的业务嫁接上去。我专门建了一个 repo，把 pi 官方文档整理归档、分类清楚，告诉你和你的 coding agent 应该怎么读、读哪些、什么时候读。"
55	
56	> "不要急着写代码。先把 pi 的文档喂对，再开始设计你的 harness。否则你配的 Agent 只会用上下文幻觉去'实现业务'，跑起来才发现到处都是坑。"
57	
58	> "AGENTS.md：给 coding agent 的铁律。进来必须先读 README + task-reading-matrix，按问题类型精准阅读 source/ 里的原始文档，回答时必须引用本地 source/ 路径，禁止凭记忆猜测 pi 行为。"
59	
60	## 局限与盲区
61	
62	- **未覆盖方面**：文章聚焦于 pi harness 的文档投喂策略，未讨论当 coding agent 读完文档后仍然产生幻觉或错误实现时的兜底方案。也未涉及实际操作中的验证流程——Agent 根据矩阵建议的 harness 设计如何被人类验证其正确性？repo 承诺"持续加真实踩坑后的 matrix"，但当前版本覆盖了多少边界场景未量化。
63	- **隐含假设**：假设 coding agent 能够有效理解并严格遵守 AGENTS.md 中的规则——但当前 coding agent 的实际行为表明，长上下文中的规则遵循仍不稳定，尤其是在复杂多步任务中。假设文档足够准确且完整，足以消除幻觉——但文档本身可能有过时或遗漏，coding agent 未必能区分"文档没说"和"不存在"。
64	- **可能的反例**：如果 pi 本身的文档质量不足以支撑精准问答（比如某些边缘行为没有文档化），那么再好的 matrix 也只是把 coding agent 指向了不完整的信息源。对于已经有大量 pi 实践经验的团队，这套玩法可能带来过度的流程开销——他们已经在踩坑中形成了自己的知识。
65	- **生态限定**：本文完全基于 pi harness 生态，不适用于选择其他 Agent 框架（如 LangGraph、CrewAI、AutoGen）的团队。方法论的通用部分（结构化文档投喂、task-reading-matrix）可以迁移，但具体 source/ 路径和 catalog/ 分类是 pi 专属的。
66	
67	## 关联
68	
69	- [[软件构建即学习]]——pi harness 业务嫁接的过程本质是学习过程，快速验证反馈循环同样适用
70	- [[离职工程师技能蒸馏]]——pi-docs-playbook 将文档知识喂给 Agent 的思路，与 dot-skill 将工程师经验喂给 Agent 的逻辑本质相同，都是对抗"人走知识走"或"文档不用知识就死"
71	- [[Claude Code动态工作流]]——pi harness 提供 Agent 运行时底座，Dynamic Workflow 提供编排层，两者在架构上互补
72	- 所属项目：[[Agent工程]]

10	---
11	# Agent Doom Loop检测与防护
12	
13	> [!abstract]- AI 摘要
14	> Doom Loop 是 Agent 持续执行但始终没有有效进展的隐蔽故障模式，不同于传统死循环，它的各项监控指标看似正常但任务进度为零。本文剖析了四种 Doom Loop 的形成机制、OpenClaw 的两道防线设计以及让长任务 Agent 真正可靠所需的五层外围基础设施。
15	
16	---
17	
18	## 扫读
19	
20	> [!tip] 💡 一句话
21	> Doom Loop 是 Agent 在 ReAct 循环中原地打转的隐蔽故障——token 在烧、日志在滚、指标都正常，但任务毫无进展，破解之道是断路器加工具循环检测两道防线，以及模型外围的状态、规划、执行 trace、验证和硬停止五层基础设施。
22	
23	> [!important] 📌 关键结论
24	> - Doom Loop 有四种典型形态：相同调用相同结果的确定性死循环、调用不存在工具的幻觉重试、轮询工具等待永不发生的事件、两个操作交替振荡的 Ping-Pong
25	> - 第一道防线——重试端断路器：上下文压缩最多 3 次，总重试硬限 32-160 次（根据候选模型数动态计算），所有错误路径共用同一计数器
26	> - 第二道防线——工具循环检测：哈希指纹 + 滑动窗口（30 条历史），两级告警（warning 提示自主纠正，critical 直接终止），覆盖四种检测器
27	> - 模型外围五层：状态（外部持久化）、规划（调度单而非 checklist）、执行 trace（工具输出落盘）、验证（机器验证 + 环境验证 + 独立评价三档）、硬停止（预算/安全边界写死）
28	> - 压缩并不能打破 Doom Loop——压缩后 Agent 会继续原工具调用再次卡死，需要压缩后开启观测窗口检测循环是否持续
29	
30	> [!quote] 🎬 可行动项
31	> - 检查现有 Agent 工作流是否实现了工具调用指纹追踪：至少记录工具名 + 参数哈希，在滑动窗口内检测重复模式
32	> - 实现两级告警阈值：同一工具同一参数 ≥10 次给 warning（让 Agent 自主纠正），≥20 次直接终止
33	> - 建立外部状态存储（progress.md 或数据库），确保任务进度、决策记录不在 context 丢失
34	> - 制定硬停止规则：任务范围扩大、预算逼近上限、验证连续失败、操作涉及删除/生产数据——这些条件写死在系统中
35	
36	---
37	
38	## 精读
39	
40	### 论证链
41	
42	现象层：Agent 运行两小时任务进度为零 —— 没有卡死、没有报错、指标正常 —— 这是 Doom Loop，和传统死循环的本质区别在于每一轮 ReAct 循环都符合模型的训练模式，Agent 自身感知不到异常。
43	
44	原因层：ReAct 循环本身没有问题，问题在于四类场景让循环失去信息增益：
45	1. 相同调用相同结果 → 确定性死循环，模型每一轮做相同决策
46	2. 幻觉工具名 → 返回"工具不存在"，Agent 解释为"暂时不可用"继续重试
47	3. 轮询卡死 → 等待永不发生的事件，Agent 不知道何时放弃
48	4. Ping-Pong → A→B→A→B 交替，每侧都"在工作"但整体无推进
49	
50	四种场景的共同本质：工具一直在调用，但每一轮都没有产出新信息。
51	
52	解决层：
53	- 第一道防线（断路器）：容错重试必须有上限，所有错误路径共享计数器
54	- 第二道防线（检测器）：哈希指纹 + 滑动窗口 + 两级告警，四种检测器覆盖四类场景
55	- 压缩后观测窗口：压缩成功不代表打破循环，需额外 3 次观测窗口验证
56	
57	升维层：Doom Loop 只是"状态、规划、验证"三位一体失控中最容易被看见的一种 —— 长任务 Agent 的根因是带不住状态、估不准工作量、评不好自己的输出。解决之道是模型外五层基础设施。
58	
59	### 关键引述
60	
61	> "Doom Loop——Agent 持续执行，却始终没有有效进展的状态。跟普通的死循环不一样。死循环 CPU 跑满、进程僵住，监视器一眼就能看出来。Doom Loop 不会：它每一步都按 ReAct 的逻辑跑，工具在调用，模型在思考，token 在烧，日志一直在滚——指标都正常，只是这些动作合起来没在推进任务。"
62	
63	> "带不住状态，估不准工作量，评不好自己的输出。这三件事一起出现，就是长任务最常见的失控链路——状态、计划、验证一起垮。"
64	
65	> "Doom Loop 是架构问题，不是模型问题。断路器和循环检测能挡掉最坏的情况，但让长任务真正可靠，还得靠上面这五层一起在线。"
66	
67	### 局限与盲区
68	
69	- 本文未覆盖：不同类型 Agent（代码生成、数据分析、对话助手）的 Doom Loop 检测阈值应如何差异化设置，文中给出的 10 次/20 次阈值是 OpenClaw 的特化参数。Ping-Pong 振荡检测中的"结果无变化"如何判定——对于返回动态数据（如时间戳、实时价格）的工具调用，简单的哈希比较会失效
70	- 隐含假设：假设 Agent 使用的是 ReAct 循环架构，对于 Plan-and-Execute、Tree-of-Thought 等其他 Agent 架构，Doom Loop 的表现形式和检测方法可能完全不同。假设工具调用的"进展"可以通过输出哈希变化来衡量，但对于渐进式任务（如逐行写入文件），每一轮输出都不同但可能无实质进展
71	- 可能的反例：某些任务确实需要大量重复调用（如批量处理、分页抓取），简单的重复计数检测会产生误报。对于探索性任务（如开放式研究），"无进展"的定义本身就是模糊的，硬性断路器可能过早终止有意义的探索
72	- 文中提出的"五层基础设施"是方向性框架，缺少每一层的具体实现模式、数据格式和集成方式，从概念到工程落地还有较大距离
73	- 未讨论在受限环境（如无文件系统访问的沙箱、Serverless）中如何实现外部状态存储
74	
75	---
76	
77	## 关联
